conceptTag: Read a café's profit and loss
readerTitle: The café sold more in June. Why did it keep less?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 카페, 온라인 원두 쇼핑몰) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 손익계산서는 매출에서 멈추지 말고 위에서 아래로 끝까지 읽는다. 매출총이익률과 순이익률을 함께 보면 돈이 어디서 새는지 보인다.
misconception: 매출이 늘었으면 장사가 잘된 것이다. 매출총이익이 늘었으면 순이익도 늘었을 것이다.

sources.text: 재무회계의 표준 개념 (손익계산서 구조, 매출총이익률, 순이익률)

cards.title: The café sold more in June. Why did it keep less?
body: A neighborhood café had its best month ever in June. Sales rose from $40,000 to $46,000.
The owner was ready to celebrate. Then she read the page to the bottom line.

image.label: Café owner reading a one-page monthly report at the counter
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 마감 후 카페 카운터에서 주인이 한 장짜리 월간 보고서를 들고 있음. 종이 맨 위 숫자는 크고 밝게, 맨 아래 숫자는 작고 흐리게. 실제 브랜드 로고나 컵 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Was June a better month?
body: In June the café added office catering and pushed iced drinks. Sales were up 15%. Gross profit, which is sales minus ingredients and cups, rose from $28,000 to $29,000.
Was June a better month for the business?

options.text: Yes. Sales grew 15%, so the café did better
options.feedback: Revenue is the top line, not what you keep. More sales can come with even more costs. That's the gap between revenue and profit.

options.text: Probably. Gross profit rose too, so profit should follow
options.feedback: A good second check, but not the last one. Gross profit rose $1,000. Costs below it can rise even more.

options.text: Can't say yet. Read down to net profit first
options.feedback: Right. Only the bottom line shows what June left after every cost. The next card shows the answer.

cards.title: Sales up 15%. Profit down 37%.
body: Net profit fell from $3,200 to $2,020. The café worked harder in June and kept about $1,180 less.

cards.title: June's profit and loss, line by line.
body: Operating costs here are wages $16,000, rent $6,000, utilities and supplies $2,000, card fees $1,380, marketing $800 and equipment wear $500. All figures are before tax.
cards.softwareNote: A software company's profit and loss reads the same way, top to bottom. The costs above gross profit are mostly servers and support, so gross margins usually run much higher.

cards.title: Each sale left less after ingredients.
body: In May, the café kept 70 cents of every dollar after ingredients. In June, it kept 63 cents. That's **gross margin**: gross profit as a share of revenue.
Catering orders got a volume discount and included sandwiches, which cost more to make than coffee. So sales rose, but each new dollar carried less profit with it.

image.label: Two coffee cups: 70% left in May, 63% left in June
image.brief: 컵 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽 "May" 컵은 70% 높이까지, 오른쪽 "June" 컵은 63% 높이까지 채워져 있음. 오른쪽 컵 옆에 샌드위치 아이콘과 "Catering discount" 작은 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The costs below gross profit grew faster.
body: Gross profit rose $1,000. But operating costs rose $2,180: about $2,000 in extra staff hours for catering, plus $180 more in card fees on higher sales.
So **net margin**, what's left after every cost, fell from 8% to 4.4%. The catering looked like growth at the top of the page. At the bottom, it cost more than it brought in.

cards.title: One page doesn't tell the whole story.
body: **One month is noisy.** A single bill or a holiday can swing it. Compare several months, or the same month last year.
**Owner pay may be missing.** Many small-business owners take no salary. If the owner works the counter for free, the real profit is lower than the page shows.
**Profit isn't cash.** The page can show a profit while the bank balance falls, for example after paying for a new grinder.

cards.title: Now it's an online coffee-bean shop.
body: Monthly sales are $60,000. Beans, packaging and shipping cost $24,000, so gross margin is 60%. Below that: ads $18,000, staff $12,000, platform and software fees $3,000, roastery rent $4,200. Net profit is −$1,200.
Where should the owner look first?

options.text: Switch to cheaper beans to raise gross margin
options.feedback: A 60% gross margin is already healthy. Cheaper beans risk the product while the real leak sits lower on the page.

options.text: The ad spend: it eats 30% of every dollar of sales
options.feedback: Reading top to bottom shows the gap opens below gross profit. Ads are the biggest line there, so that's where net margin is lost.
Higher prices would lift both margins, but some customers may leave. It treats the symptom before finding the cause.

cards.softwareNote: This is a common pattern for online sellers: strong gross margins, with customer-acquisition costs quietly erasing the bottom line.

cards.title: Read the page to the bottom, then ask where the gap opened.
body: You used three ideas today: **revenue vs profit** (more sales isn't more money kept), the **income statement** read top to bottom, and **gross vs net margin** to find where profit leaked.
**Try it today:** take your last two months' profit and loss. Work out gross margin and net margin for each. Which one moved more?
